# Part 2 · Shape, color, and a trend line

> 🔮 **Predict first:** We map `color = shade` and `shape = shade` to the same variable. One legend or two?

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# scatter of mass vs petiole length, one color + shape per shade
leaf_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = petiole_mm, y = mass_g, color = shade, shape = shade)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("sunny" = "goldenrod", "shady" = "forestgreen")) +
  labs(
    title = "Leaf Mass vs. Petiole Length",
    x = "Petiole Length (mm)", y = "Leaf Mass (g)",
    color = "Shade", shape = "Shade"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

✏️ **Your turn — in your script:** Add a `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` layer to the plot above (no color/fill needed — let it default). Run it.

```         
Does the trend line slope up or down?
```

> ✅ **You can already do a lot:** a colored, shaped, labelled scatter with a trend line. Parts 3–5 are polish — zooming, themes, and saving.

# Part 3 · Zoom in safely with `coord_cartesian()`

Sometimes a handful of extreme points squash the rest of the data into a corner and you want a closer look. `coord_cartesian()` zooms the **view** and leaves the data alone — every leaf still counts toward the trend line.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# zoom the view; all 53 leaves still contribute to the trend line
leaf_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = petiole_mm, y = mass_g)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "tomato") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(50, 70)) +
  labs(title = "Zoomed with coord_cartesian()",
       x = "Petiole Length (mm)", y = "Leaf Mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

✏️ **Your turn — in your script:** Change the window to `coord_cartesian(xlim = c(55, 65))` and run it. The view gets tighter — does the trend line itself move?

```         
Did the line move?
```

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ The classic mistake: `xlim()` / `ylim()` delete rows**

`xlim()` and `ylim()` look like they just zoom, but they **silently drop every row outside the range** *before* anything is calculated. A trend line added after `xlim()` is fit only on the leaves that survived — so it can point a different direction, with no warning that data went missing.

**Rule:** zoom with `coord_cartesian()`. Only reach for `xlim()` / `ylim()` when you actually want those rows removed from the analysis.
:::

**▶ Run this once to see the trap:**

``` r
# same plot, but xlim() drops the outside rows FIRST — watch the line change
leaf_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = petiole_mm, y = mass_g)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "tomato") +
  xlim(50, 70) +
  labs(title = "xlim() — trend line refit on fewer leaves",
       x = "Petiole Length (mm)", y = "Leaf Mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```         
Compared with the coord_cartesian() version, did this trend line move?
```

# Part 4 · Pick a theme

**▶ Run this — build the plot once, then try two themes:**

``` r
# base plot, no theme yet
leaf_plot <- leaf_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = shade, y = mass_g, fill = shade)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("sunny" = "goldenrod", "shady" = "forestgreen")) +
  labs(x = "Shade", y = "Leaf Mass (g)", title = "Leaf Mass by Shade")

leaf_plot + theme_minimal()    # light, faint gridlines
leaf_plot + theme_classic()    # axis lines only — close to journal style
```

```         
Which of the two do you prefer for a figure in a report?
```

### One small tweak with `theme()`

Pick a base theme, then use `theme()` to override single pieces. The most common tweak is dropping a legend you don't need (here `fill` just repeats the x-axis):

``` r
leaf_plot_final <- leaf_plot +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

leaf_plot_final
```

✏️ **Your turn — in your script:** Add `plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")` inside `theme()` and run it.

# Part 5 · Save in two formats

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# PNG for slides and web, PDF for print / vector editing
ggsave("figures/leaf_mass_theme.png",
       plot = leaf_plot_final, width = 5, height = 5,
       units = "in", dpi = 300)

ggsave("figures/leaf_mass_theme.pdf",
       plot = leaf_plot_final, width = 5, height = 5, units = "in")
```

```         
Open both files. When would you send a colleague the .pdf instead of the .png?
```

## E1 · See exactly what `xlim()` removes (5 pts)

Stay with `mass_g` vs `petiole_mm` and the window from Part 3 (`50` to `70`).

1.  Run `nrow(leaf_df)` — the full leaf count.
2.  Run `leaf_df %>% filter(petiole_mm >= 50, petiole_mm <= 70) %>% nrow()` — how many leaves land *inside* the window. That is the number `xlim(50, 70)` silently keeps.
3.  Build the scatter with `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` **twice** — once with `coord_cartesian(xlim = c(50, 70))`, once with `xlim(50, 70)`.

In comments, record both counts and whether the two trend lines pointed the same way.

## E2 · Explain it (5 pts)

In two or three sentences, using your two row counts: why did `xlim()` produce a different trend line than `coord_cartesian()`? Then give one realistic example where silently dropping rows like this would lead a scientist to the wrong conclusion.

# Getting unstuck

1.  **Read the error message out loud.** R usually names the line and the problem.
2.  **Trend line looks wrong after zooming?** Check whether you used `xlim()`/`ylim()` (deletes data) instead of `coord_cartesian()` (keeps it).
3.  **Legend didn't merge?** `color` and `shape` (and the matching `labs()` titles) must all reference the exact same variable name.
4.  **Cheat sheets** — <https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/>
5.  **Bring the exact error** (copy-paste it) to class, Canvas, or office hours.
